transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess I'm here because things at home have been... tense. I know my wife says the late meetings and these little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It's like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

It actually reminds me a lot of how the administration communicates at the university. I'm a teaching assistant, and they just changed our whole grading portal without telling anyone. Typical, right? I spent three hours yesterday just trying to input midterm scores. The students get so panicked if their grades aren't up immediately. When I was doing my graduate work, we had to wait weeks for a paper to come back, and we survived just fine. Though, to be fair, I did spend most of that time in the library cafe. They had these incredible blueberry scones... I wonder if they still make them. The baker there used real butter, you could always tell. 

But, uh, anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, my wife just thought it would be a good idea for me to come in and talk to someone.
Do you believe for certain that your wife’s work messages contain hidden signals meant specifically for you?

I mean, yes, absolutely. Like I was just saying, if you look at a whole year of these late meetings and the little shifts in how she writes her messages, it’s just too precise to be an accident. I know she claims it's just normal office stuff, but it's clearly a private signal meant for me. She's trying to tell me something without actually saying it out loud. 

It’s a lot like analyzing literature, really. You have to look at the subtext. I try to teach my students about subtext, but getting them to even read the main text is a battle these days. Just last week, I had a sophomore ask if they could listen to a podcast instead of reading the assigned journal article. A podcast! I mean, I do listen to podcasts when I commute—there's a really good one about the history of the Roman Empire, the host does all these different voices for the historical figures—but you can't cite a podcast in a serious research paper. Well, actually, maybe you can with the new APA guidelines. They change the formatting rules every few years anyway. It's completely impossible to keep track of where the commas are supposed to go now. 

But, um... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my wife's emails. Yeah, I'm certain there's a hidden message in them.
Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?

Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. It's just the messages, the patterns in the text. I mean, my hearing is perfectly fine. Actually, I think it might be a little too good sometimes. The walls in our apartment building are incredibly thin. The couple next door just got a new puppy, and I swear I can hear every time its little claws click against their hardwood floor. It’s a beagle, I think. They have that very distinct, sort of mournful howl. 

My uncle used to have a beagle when I was growing up. Buster, his name was. He was an absolute menace, always getting into the trash. We had to put these childproof locks on all the lower cabinets just to keep him out of the kitchen. Uncle Frank got so frustrated once that he tried to build this elaborate wooden barricade, but Buster just chewed right through it. Frank was a carpenter, too, so you'd think he would have built something sturdier. He made this beautiful oak dining table for my parents as a wedding gift. It’s still in their dining room, actually, not a single scratch on it after forty years. 

Wait, what did you ask me? Something about hearing things? No, no voices. Just the regular apartment noise.
Do people often tell you that your speech is hard to follow because you go off on tangents?

Hard to follow? I don't think so. I mean, my wife sometimes sighs and says I'm taking the long way around to a point, but I think that's just because I like to give context. Context is everything, especially in my field. You can't just read a historical document without understanding the political climate of the time. It's like trying to understand the French Revolution without knowing about the bread shortages. 

Actually, I tried making my own sourdough bread during the pandemic, like everyone else did. I got this starter going—I named him Dough-B-Wan Kenobi, my students thought that was hilarious—and I kept him alive for a solid eight months. But then we had that awful heatwave last summer, and our building's AC went out for three days. It was unbearable. I tried putting the starter in the fridge to slow it down, but I think I shocked it or something. It just never bubbled the same way after that. It's a shame, too, because I was getting really good at scoring the top of the loaves. I bought one of those special little razor blades on a stick... a lame, I think it's called? It's a French word. 

Anyway, sorry, you were asking if people say I'm hard to follow? No, not really. I think I communicate pretty clearly, all things considered.
Do you ever feel that your thoughts are being put into your mind by someone else?

Put into my mind? No, no, they're my thoughts. I mean, nobody's beaming things into my head or anything like that. My thoughts are my own, they just... they just get a little busy sometimes, you know? Like a crowded highway. 

Speaking of highways, the traffic on I-95 this morning was just atrocious. I don't know why they decided to do construction on the southbound lane right during rush hour. It backed up for miles. I was sitting there, listening to the radio, and they were playing this old jazz station. I used to play the saxophone in high school, actually. Alto sax. I wasn't very good, but I loved the shiny brass. My parents rented it for me from this little music shop downtown that smelled like cork grease and old paper. The owner, Mr. Henderson, he had this huge collection of vintage metronomes. Just shelves and shelves of them ticking away. It was almost hypnotic, standing in there. 

I tried to find a metronome app for my phone the other day, just to help me pace my grading, but they all have these annoying ads that pop up right when you're trying to focus. It's impossible to concentrate when you're suddenly getting yelled at to buy car insurance. 

Um, but what were you asking? Oh, about thoughts being put in my head? No, definitely not. Just my own thoughts in there.
Have you tended to avoid other people because you feel uncomfortable or suspicious around them?

Avoid people? Uncomfortable? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still go to work, I still see my students. I hold office hours every Tuesday and Thursday. It's just that lately, not as many students have been showing up. Which is fine, really, it gives me more time to focus on my own research. 

I've been looking into the trade routes of the Hanseatic League in the 14th century. It's fascinating how much power a merchant guild could wield over entire nations. They practically controlled the Baltic Sea. I actually took a trip to Lübeck a few years ago, before the pandemic. Beautiful city. The Holstentor—that big brick gate—it's just stunning in person. They have this incredible marzipan there, too. Niederegger, I think the brand is called. My wife loves marzipan, so I brought back this huge assortment box. It had all these different flavors... pistachio, espresso, orange. We kept it in the pantry, but I think the humidity got to it eventually, because the last few pieces went a bit stale. 

It's funny how humidity affects things. Like the pages of old books, they get all wavy if you don't store them right. The library at the university has this special climate-controlled rare book room. You have to wear these little white cotton gloves if you want to handle anything in there. I always feel like a magician when I put them on. 

Wait, sorry, what was the question? Something about avoiding people? No, I'm fine around people. Just busy with my work, mostly.
Have these beliefs about your wife’s messages caused problems with how you function at work or at home?

Well, at work, no, not really. I'm still doing my job, keeping my routines, grading papers, making sure I shower and all that. But at home... yeah, it's been tense. My wife and I have had these repeated, really strained conversations about it. It actually got to the point where our couples therapist suggested I come get an individual assessment. 

Therapy is strange, isn't it? Sitting on those couches. Ours has this patterned upholstery that looks exactly like the curtains my grandmother had in her living room back in Ohio. She had this huge bay window where she kept African violets. Dozens of them, in these little clay pots. You have to be so careful watering them, you know, because if you get water on the leaves, they rot. You have to water them from the bottom. She had these special little saucers for every single pot. I tried keeping an African violet once in my office, but the fluorescent lights just didn't agree with it. It got all leggy and sad looking. I ended up giving it to the department secretary, Linda. She has a real green thumb. Her desk looks like a jungle. She's got this pothos plant that practically wraps around her computer monitor. 

I always wonder how she cleans her desk with all those vines everywhere. Dusting must be a nightmare. I hate dusting. I have asthma, so dust really gets to me if I'm not careful. 

But anyway, to answer your question... yeah, it's mostly just caused problems in my marriage, not really with my work or anything else.
For how long have you been certain that your wife’s messages contain hidden signals for you?

Well, it's been about a year now. I'd say it really started right around the time she went back to working outside the home again. She took a job at this architectural firm downtown, right off 4th Street. 

It's a beautiful building they're in, actually. Art Deco. Built in the late twenties, I think. It has these incredible brass elevator doors with geometric patterns etched into them. I've always loved Art Deco architecture. The Chrysler Building in New York is probably my favorite. I went to New York once, years ago, for an academic conference. We stayed in this hotel near Times Square, and the noise was just unbelievable. Sirens all night long. I don't know how people live with that constant racket. I need quiet to sleep. I even use a white noise machine at home, the kind with the actual mechanical fan inside, not the digital loops. The digital ones always have this subtle click when the track repeats, and once I hear it, I just fixate on it and can't fall asleep. 

My wife says she can't even hear the click, but she sleeps like a log anyway. She could sleep through an earthquake. We actually had a minor tremor here about a decade ago, rattled the dishes in the cupboards, and she didn't even stir. 

But yeah, the hidden signals... it's been about a year, since she started that new job.
Aside from your wife’s messages, do you believe there are other hidden messages meant specifically for you?

No, no, just the text messages. It's only her messages that have those signals. I don't look for them anywhere else, you know, like in the newspaper or on the radio or anything. 

I still listen to the radio, actually. A lot of people just use Spotify or whatever, but I like NPR. Especially on Sunday mornings. They have this puzzle segment with Will Shortz. I try to figure out the word puzzles while I'm making breakfast. I usually make oatmeal on Sundays. Steel-cut oats, not the instant kind. The instant kind gets too mushy, almost like paste. You have to simmer the steel-cut ones for a good twenty minutes, but the texture is so much better. I like to put a little brown sugar and some toasted pecans on top. 

Pecans are getting so expensive, though. I went to the grocery store last week—the one over on Elm Street, because the one closer to our house never has decent produce—and a little bag of pecans was almost nine dollars. Nine dollars! It's ridiculous. I ended up buying walnuts instead. They're not quite the same, a little more bitter, I think. But they work in a pinch. 

My grandfather had a huge walnut tree in his backyard when I was growing up. We used to spend hours picking them up in the fall. Your hands would get stained this dark brownish-black color from the husks, and it wouldn't wash off for days. My mother hated it. She'd scrub my hands with a pumice stone until they were raw. 

But no, just her texts. Nothing else.
Have you ever felt that someone was controlling your actions?

No, I've never felt anything like that. I'm the one making my choices, doing my grading, going to work. No one's pulling my strings or anything. 

Speaking of strings, though, my wife bought this marionette puppet when we were in Prague on our honeymoon. It's a beautifully carved wooden thing, a jester with these little bells on its hat. They have these amazing puppet shops all over Prague, just windows full of them. The craftsmanship is really something. But the strings on this one get tangled so easily. I tried to untangle them once, and it took me almost an hour. It's like trying to untangle old Christmas lights. 

We actually need to buy new Christmas lights this year. The ones we have are those old incandescent bulbs, and half of them burn out every time you plug them in. It's so frustrating trying to find the one bad bulb that's making the whole strand go dark. I think I'm just going to switch to LEDs this year. They're supposed to last longer and use less electricity. Plus, they don't get hot. I always worry about those old bulbs starting a fire on a dry tree. 

We usually get a real tree, a Fraser fir. The smell is just incredible. Fake trees just don't have that same magic, you know? They just smell like plastic and dust. 

But no, to get back to what you asked, nobody is controlling my actions. I'm completely in control of myself.
Before this started with your wife’s messages, had anyone ever told you that your speech or behavior seemed odd or eccentric?

No, no one's ever said anything like that to me. I've always been pretty normal, I think. Just a regular guy, going about my business, grading papers... 

I grade a lot of papers, actually. Being a teaching assistant for the intro history classes means I'm buried in essays by midterms. The students these days, though, their writing skills are just atrocious. It's like they've never been taught how to construct a proper paragraph, let alone a cohesive argument. They rely so much on spellcheck and grammar apps, but those programs don't catch everything. They certainly don't teach you how to think critically. 

I was reading this article the other day about how handwriting is becoming a lost art. It's really a shame. I always use a fountain pen when I'm grading. A Lamy Safari, charcoal black, with a fine nib. It just glides across the paper. There's something so satisfying about the physical act of writing with a good pen. You have to use the right ink, though. I prefer a deep, rich blue, like a sapphire. The cheap inks tend to feather and bleed through the paper, especially on the thin notebook paper the students use. 

I remember when I was in grade school, we actually had penmanship classes. We had to practice making those perfect cursive loops for hours. My teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was a stickler for neatness. If you smudged your ink, you had to start the whole page over. She had this enormous collection of brooches, a different one for every day of the month, I swear. One was shaped like a little silver owl with green glass eyes. I used to stare at it while she was lecturing about the Civil War. 

But no, to answer your question, nobody has ever told me I act odd or eccentric. I'm just me.
Did this tendency to go off on tangents in conversation start around the same time as the concerns about your wife’s messages, or was it already there long before that?

Tangents? I don't really think I go off on tangents. I mean, I just talk the way I've always talked. I've always been a bit of a storyteller, I guess. It's not a new thing. 

Speaking of stories, my grandfather was the best storyteller. He used to sit on the porch—he had this old wooden rocking chair that squeaked every time he leaned back—and he'd tell us these elaborate tales about his time in the Navy. He was stationed in the Pacific during the Korean War. He had this one story about a typhoon that hit their ship, and the waves were so high they crashed right over the deck. He said the whole ship pitched so far to one side he thought they were going to capsize. 

I've always wanted to go on a cruise, actually. Maybe not to the Pacific, but somewhere calm, like the Caribbean. My wife and I looked into it for our tenth anniversary, but we couldn't decide on an itinerary. She wanted to go to the Bahamas, but I was leaning more towards the Southern Caribbean—Aruba, Curaçao, those islands down by South America. The water there is supposed to be this incredible, crystal-clear turquoise. 

I saw a documentary on PBS the other night about coral reefs in the Caribbean. It's really depressing how much of the coral is dying off because of the water temperatures rising. They showed these huge stretches of reef that were just completely bleached white, like a graveyard. It makes you wonder what the oceans are going to look like in fifty years. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I don't think my talking has changed at all. I've always just been conversational.
Before the past year, did you ever have unusual beliefs or experiences that other people found strange?

No, I don't think so. I've never had any beliefs that people thought were strange. I've always just been a pretty grounded person, you know? Focused on my work, my research... 

I'm doing my dissertation on the economic impacts of the Erie Canal. It's fascinating stuff, really. A lot of people think of it just as a transportation route, but the way it transformed the local economies of the towns along the route—places like Rochester and Syracuse—it's just incredible. Rochester actually became known as the "Flour City" because of all the mills that sprang up. 

I actually tried to bake my own bread a few weeks ago. Sourdough. Everyone was doing it a couple of years ago, and I finally decided to give it a try. Making the starter is the hardest part. You have to feed it every day, like a pet. It smells kind of like beer after a while. I used this organic rye flour I found at the farmer's market. The farmer's market downtown is great, they have this one stand that sells the most amazing heirloom tomatoes in the summer. The big, ugly ones that taste incredible. 

Anyway, the bread turned out okay, a little dense, maybe. I think I didn't let it proof long enough. Baking is so precise, it's really more like chemistry than cooking. If your water is too hot, you kill the yeast. 

But no, I've never had any unusual beliefs or anything like that. Just normal stuff.
Has your wife ever actually admitted that her messages contain hidden signals for you?

No, she hasn't admitted it. She always just says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. But for the past year, they’ve lined up way too precisely to feel accidental, you know? It's like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she just won’t say directly. 

It reminds me of cryptography, actually. During World War II, the Navajo code talkers were instrumental in the Pacific theater. The Japanese couldn't crack their language because it was so complex and unwritten at the time. I read this fascinating biography on Alan Turing, too, and his work at Bletchley Park cracking the Enigma machine. The sheer mathematical genius it took to build the Bombe machine to decipher those daily German codes... it's mind-boggling. 

I've always been pretty good at math, actually, even though history is my main focus. I used to do those Sudoku puzzles in the Sunday paper every week. My dad used to do the crossword. He’d sit there with his black coffee—always black, he said milk ruined the flavor of a good roast—and he wouldn't speak to anyone until he finished the puzzle. He used a pen, too, never a pencil. He said using a pencil meant you lacked confidence in your answers. 

I tried getting into those cryptic crosswords they have in the British papers, but they're a completely different beast. You really have to think laterally. But anyway, no, she hasn't admitted it. I just know there's something there she isn't telling me.
Do you believe your wife is having an affair?

An affair? No, no, I don't think it's an affair. I don't get the sense that there's another man involved or anything like that. It's more about the messages themselves, the structure of them, you know? 

Speaking of structure, I was looking at the architecture of that new library downtown the other day. It's got this incredible brutalist design. Lots of exposed concrete and harsh angles. It's a very polarizing style. A lot of people think it looks like a parking garage, but I actually appreciate the honesty of the materials. It originated in the 1950s, mostly in the UK, as a way to rebuild quickly and cheaply after the war. 

I took a trip to London when I was an undergrad. We stayed in this tiny hostel near King's Cross. The tube is so much more efficient than the subway system in New York. We took the train all the way out to Greenwich to see the Royal Observatory. Standing on the Prime Meridian line is a strange feeling, knowing you're straddling two hemispheres. 

We had fish and chips at this little pub near the river. They wrapped it in actual newspaper, which I guess is the traditional way to do it, though you wonder about the ink getting on the food. The vinegar they put on it is so strong, it almost takes your breath away. 

But no, I don't think she's having an affair. It's just... the signals. They mean something else entirely.
What do you think the hidden signals in your wife’s messages are trying to tell you?

I'm... not entirely sure, honestly. That's the frustrating part. I know they mean *something*, but I haven't quite figured out the exact message yet. It's like having a word on the tip of your tongue, you know? 

It reminds me of when I was trying to learn French before a trip to Montreal a few years ago. I got one of those language learning apps, the ones with the little owl that guilts you if you miss a day. It's a very clever psychological trick, really, gamifying the learning process. You get these little streaks and badges. 

Montreal is a beautiful city, by the way. The old town, Vieux-Montréal, feels like you've stepped into Europe. The cobblestone streets are murder on your ankles if you aren't wearing the right shoes, though. I bought these expensive walking shoes before the trip, but they gave me terrible blisters on the first day. I ended up wearing my old, beat-up sneakers for the rest of the week. 

We went to this little bistro and I tried to order in French, but the waiter just immediately switched to English. I guess my accent was that bad. They have this amazing dish there, poutine. It sounds awful—french fries covered in cheese curds and brown gravy—but it's incredible, especially if it's cold outside. And it was freezing. The wind coming off the St. Lawrence River just cuts right through you. 

But yeah, the signals. I haven't cracked them yet. I just know they're there.
What exactly do you think the hidden signals in your wife’s messages are about?

Like I said, I really wish I could give you a straight answer on that. I just don't know what the subject is yet. I haven't deciphered the core meaning, just the pattern. It's incredibly frustrating, actually. It's a bit like trying to find the thesis statement in the essays my undergrads turn in. 

I'm a teaching assistant for a 200-level European History course this semester, and honestly, you wouldn't believe the leaps in logic these sophomores make. Just last week, I was grading their midterms on the French Revolution. I had this one student—nice kid, always sits in the second row, always wearing this bright neon orange beanie, even indoors. I didn't think hats were allowed in the main lecture hall, but Professor Davis never says anything about it, so I let it slide. Anyway, this kid wrote an entire page arguing that Marie Antoinette was just a victim of poor supply chain management. Supply chain management! In 1789! I mean, I suppose you could look at the Parisian grain shortages that way if you really stretched it, but he was using all these modern corporate buzzwords. It was like reading a LinkedIn post about the Reign of Terror. 

I had to drink three cups of green tea just to get through that stack of blue books. I've been trying to switch to tea and cut back on coffee lately. Coffee makes my heart race if I have it after noon, and it really messes with my sleep schedule. I read this article the other day about how caffeine binds to the adenosine receptors in your brain, preventing you from feeling tired, but it doesn't actually give you energy, it just masks the exhaustion. 

But, um, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my wife's messages. Yeah, no, I don't know exactly what they're about yet. I'm still trying to put the pieces together.
Do you think it is actually possible for your wife to be hiding messages in those texts, or does it seem impossible for anyone to do that in a normal way?

Well, sure it's possible. I mean, I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but... well, speaking of office stuff, the departmental office in the history building has been a complete nightmare lately. The main copier has been broken for three weeks. Three weeks! It's this massive Kyocera machine, and the repair tech keeps saying he's waiting on a part from Germany. 

Germany makes incredible machinery, though, you have to admit. I drove a Volkswagen Jetta for, gosh, ten years. Fantastic car, right up until the transmission died on the interstate. Have you ever been stuck on the shoulder of a major highway in the pouring rain? It is absolutely terrifying. The semi-trucks just fly past you, spraying water so hard it feels like the car is going to tip over. I waited two hours for the tow truck. The driver was this really fascinating guy, actually—he used to be a semi-pro bowler in the late nineties before he hurt his wrist. He was explaining the physics of how the oil patterns on the wood lanes affect the hook of the ball. It's incredibly precise, how you have to calculate the angles.

Which, I guess, brings me back to the texts. Because for the past year, the changes in her messages... they’ve just lined up too precisely to feel accidental. Statistically, it just doesn't make sense as a coincidence. It really feels like there’s a private signal in them, like they're meant to tell me something she just won’t say directly.
Has anyone at work or home told you recently that your speech has become hard to follow?

No, nobody's said anything like that. Why, do I sound hard to follow? I feel like I'm communicating just fine. I mean, my students understand me, mostly. Well, except for that one kid with the orange beanie, but I think that's more of a listening comprehension issue on his part. 

Listening comprehension is actually fascinating when you think about it. The way the brain processes auditory signals and translates them into semantic meaning... I was reading a paper on it the other day. It was published in this obscure linguistics journal. My wife actually suggested I read it. She knows I love that kind of stuff. She’s an editor for a small publishing house downtown. They do a lot of academic texts, mostly sociology and political science. It’s a tough industry right now, publishing. Everyone wants everything digital, and the profit margins on physical books are just razor-thin. 

She used to bring home these advance reader copies all the time, these thick paperbacks with plain covers. I used to read them on the train. I take the Red Line in every morning, and it’s usually pretty quiet before 7 AM. You get the real early birds, the construction workers, the nurses coming off the night shift. There’s this one guy who always gets on at my stop, always carries a battered old leather briefcase. I've always wondered what's in it. It looks heavy. 

But anyway, no, my speech is fine. No one's complained about it. I'm perfectly clear.
Over the past year, have you become less interested in things you used to enjoy?

No, not really. I still enjoy the same things. I still love history, obviously, and reading. Though I haven't been reading on the train as much lately. The Red Line has been having all these signal issues, so it's been really jerky and stop-and-go. It makes it hard to focus on a page when you're getting thrown against the plastic seats every two minutes. 

Those seats are so uncomfortable, by the way. I don't know who designed them, but they clearly didn't have human anatomy in mind. It's like they used a rigid mold of a crash test dummy and just called it a day. Speaking of crash test dummies, did you know that for decades they only used male models for crash testing? It's true! They didn't start using female crash test dummies until fairly recently, which meant that women were getting injured in car accidents at much higher rates because the safety features weren't designed for their bodies. It's a fascinating, albeit depressing, example of systemic bias in engineering. 

I was actually thinking about incorporating that into a lecture sometime, maybe if I ever get to teach a course on the history of technology and society. I've been sketching out a syllabus for it in my free time. It's a lot of fun, putting together a reading list. You have to balance the dense academic theory with accessible narratives, otherwise the undergrads just check out completely. 

But yeah, to answer your question, my interests haven't really changed. I'm still doing all the stuff I normally do.

The semi-trucks just fly past you, spraying water so hard it feels like the car is going to tip over. I waited two hours for the tow truck. The driver was this really fascinating guy, actually—he used to be a semi-pro bowler in the late nineties before he hurt his wrist. He was explaining the physics of how the oil patterns on the wood lanes affect the hook of the ball. It's incredibly precise, how you have to calculate the angles.

Which, I guess, brings me back to the texts. Because for the past year, the changes in her messages... they’ve just lined up too precisely to feel accidental. Statistically, it just doesn't make sense as a coincidence. It really feels like there’s a private signal in them, like they're meant to tell me something she just won’t say directly.

doctor.intent: Determine whether his odd, tangential speech and probable thought disorder are present only in the context of a fixed delusional belief or reflect a broader persistent psychotic/disorganized syndrome, helping distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia/schizotypal conditions.
doctor.question: Has anyone at work or home told you recently that your speech has become hard to follow?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about disorganized speech (whether others have found the patient's speech hard to follow), which is a symptom of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders, but it is not covered in the provided symptom profiles for this patient with Delusional Disorder.

patient.answer:
No, nobody's said anything like that. Why, do I sound hard to follow? I feel like I'm communicating just fine. I mean, my students understand me, mostly. Well, except for that one kid with the orange beanie, but I think that's more of a listening comprehension issue on his part. 

Listening comprehension is actually fascinating when you think about it. The way the brain processes auditory signals and translates them into semantic meaning... I was reading a paper on it the other day. It was published in this obscure linguistics journal. My wife actually suggested I read it. She knows I love that kind of stuff. She’s an editor for a small publishing house downtown. They do a lot of academic texts, mostly sociology and political science. It’s a tough industry right now, publishing. Everyone wants everything digital, and the profit margins on physical books are just razor-thin. 

She used to bring home these advance reader copies all the time, these thick paperbacks with plain covers. I used to read them on the train. I take the Red Line in every morning, and it’s usually pretty quiet before 7 AM. You get the real early birds, the construction workers, the nurses coming off the night shift. There’s this one guy who always gets on at my stop, always carries a battered old leather briefcase. I've always wondered what's in it. It looks heavy. 

But anyway, no, my speech is fine. No one's complained about it. I'm perfectly clear.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are persistent negative symptoms or deterioration in functioning suggestive of schizophrenia rather than delusional disorder or schizotypal personality disorder.
doctor.question: Over the past year, have you become less interested in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a decrease in interest in previously enjoyed activities (anhedonia/apathy, a negative symptom of schizophrenia or a symptom of depression). The symptom profiles provided do not include anhedonia or a decrease in interest.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I still enjoy the same things. I still love history, obviously, and reading. Though I haven't been reading on the train as much lately. The Red Line has been having all these signal issues, so it's been really jerky and stop-and-go. It makes it hard to focus on a page when you're getting thrown against the plastic seats every two minutes. 

Those seats are so uncomfortable, by the way. I don't know who designed them, but they clearly didn't have human anatomy in mind. It's like they used a rigid mold of a crash test dummy and just called it a day. Speaking of crash test dummies, did you know that for decades they only used male models for crash testing? It's true! They didn't start using female crash test dummies until fairly recently, which meant that women were getting injured in car accidents at much higher rates because the safety features weren't designed for their bodies. It's a fascinating, albeit depressing, example of systemic bias in engineering. 

I was actually thinking about incorporating that into a lecture sometime, maybe if I ever get to teach a course on the history of technology and society. I've been sketching out a syllabus for it in my free time. It's a lot of fun, putting together a reading list. You have to balance the dense academic theory with accessible narratives, otherwise the undergrads just check out completely. 

But yeah, to answer your question, my interests haven't really changed. I'm still doing all the stuff I normally do.

opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory/referential delusional belief for about 1 year that his wife's messages contain hidden signals specifically for him, with high conviction despite her denial. Functioning is largely preserved outside the marital conflict, and there are no hallucinations, thought insertion/control, negative symptoms, broad deterioration, or other clear schizophrenic symptoms. Longstanding circumstantial/tangential style appears trait-like rather than new psychotic disorganization. This pattern best fits persistent delusional disorder.
